long_form.title_primary: How Two Brothers Bought Up Half the World's Silver
title_challengers: Two Brothers Once Bought Up Half the World's Silver
The Day the Richest Men in America Ran Out of Cash
long_form.description:
In 1980, two Texas brothers bought up about half the world's tradeable silver and drove the price from under $10 to nearly $50 an ounce. Then it all came apart in a single afternoon.

Nelson Bunker Hunt thought paper money was a con, so he set out to trade his family's oil fortune for something a government couldn't print: silver. Buying much of it on borrowed money, the Hunt brothers ended up holding roughly half the silver anyone could actually buy, built a paper fortune of nearly $7 billion, and nearly took Wall Street down with them. This is how the corner actually worked, why the exchange changed the rules to stop it, how the same leverage that built the empire destroyed it on Silver Thursday, and why the hard-money crusaders who thought the system was a fraud had to be rescued by a $1 billion bank bailout.

Sources:
- "Silver Thursday," Wikipedia (drawing on the SEC/CFTC record): the ~195-million-ounce hoard, the futures-and-leverage mechanism, the price path (under $10 to ~$34 by end-1979 to nearly $50 in January 1980), the position value (~$1.1B to ~$6.8B), the COMEX liquidation-only rule change, Silver Thursday (27 March 1980, ~$10.80), the ~$122M broker debit, the ~$1.1B thirteen-bank bailout loan, the 1988 conspiracy-to-corner verdict, the 1988 bankruptcy, and the 1989 CFTC trading bar.
- Reporting on how much of the market the Hunts held (Liberty Gold Silver; the CFTC characterization of the privately-held supply): the ~195 million ounces as about half the world's deliverable silver.
- Priceonomics, "How the Hunt Brothers Cornered the Silver Market and Then Lost it All," and Silver Monthly, "Bunker Hunt's Attraction to Silver": the 1973 silver airlift to Switzerland under armed guard, Bunker Hunt's John Birch anti-government worldview and frugal habits, and the hard-money motive.

primary.concept: Pairs with 'How Two Brothers Bought Up Half the World's Silver.' One dominant object: a towering, neatly stacked mountain of silver bars, clean 2.5D vector, flat cel shading, on a single-color field with ~60% negative space, no face. The one red accent is a red arrow crashing down the side of the stack. Overlay '$50 to $11' is the peak-to-crash price, so title (they bought up half the silver) and thumbnail (and it collapsed) open the loop together without either restating the other.

challengers.concept: Pairs with 'Two Brothers Once Bought Up Half the World's Silver.' One dominant object: a single lonely silver bar sitting in an otherwise empty open bank vault, clean 2.5D vector, flat cel, single-color field, >=60% negative space, no face. The one red accent is a small red bankruptcy/overdue stamp on the vault door. Overlay 'Then: broke' delivers the reversal the 'once' in the title hints at, not a restatement.

Pairs with 'The Day the Richest Men in America Ran Out of Cash.' One dominant composition: two Texan cowboy hats resting on top of a large pile of silver bars, with an empty leather wallet flopped open beside them, clean 2.5D vector, flat cel, single-color field, >=55% negative space, no face. The one red accent is a small red margin-call notice tucked into the pile. Overlay 'Out of cash' names the paradox (richest men, no cash) rather than repeating the title.

long_form.pinned_comment: The part that still gets me: the brothers spent a decade and a fortune insisting paper money was a fraud, and then were saved from ruin by a billion-dollar loan of exactly that. Do you read the exchange switching to sell-only as a fair move to stop a corner, or the house quietly protecting its own players who were on the losing side of the bet?

ab_experiment.note: YouTube Studio-only (Test & Compare, desktop, long-form). Data API v3 cannot submit this. Set up manually: pick title_primary+challengers and thumbnail primary+challengers. The three test genuinely different framings within the locked vindication / forbidden-knowledge lever — (primary) the audacious premise (two brothers bought up half the world's silver), (challenger 1) the premise-plus-reversal ('once' bought it, then broke), (challenger 2) the irony/fall hook (the richest men in America ran out of cash).
